WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Congress passed a $300 billion farm bill over President Bush's veto for a second time Wednesday, a step made necessary by a clerical error when the original bill passed. Congress overrode President Bush's second veto of a $300 billion farm bill. The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over Bush's objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both votes were well above the two-thirds majority needed to override the veto, which Bush delivered Wednesday morning. Congress overrode an earlier veto of the farm bill last month, even though lawmakers had discovered that 34 pages were missing in the version originally sent to the White House. In spiking the latest version, Bush said he objected to its continued subsidies for the wealthy and its use of budget gimmicks to hide a $20 billion increase in spending. But Sen. Kent Conrad, the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, said the measure actually saves the government $110 million. "This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," he said. "That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office." The discovery of the missing section, Title III, prompted concerns from House Republicans that the override vote was improper. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the sections of the bill that were originally sent to the president had become law after Congress voted to override Bush's first veto. But to put Title III into effect, Congress re-passed the entire legislation, including the missing pages, and resent it to Bush. The House voted 306-110 at the end of May. The Senate voted 77-15 for the bill at the beginning of June. Two-thirds of the $300 billion in spending for the farm bill will go for nutrition programs such as food stamps. Another $40 billion will go toward farm subsidies, and $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle and other environmental programs. After vetoing the latest version of the farm bill, Bush scolded Congress on Wednesday for not "modifying certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message." When he vetoed the first version of the farm bill, Bush said it "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." The president said it would hurt efforts to improve American farmers' access to overseas markets. Congress has passed one other bill over Bush's objections: legislation for a $23 billion water project that the president vetoed in 2007. CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Congress on Wednesday passed a $300 billion farm bill over President Bush’s veto for a second time, a step necessitated by a clerical error in the original legislation.

The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over Bush’s objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both margins were well above the two-thirds majority required to override a presidential veto, which Bush issued Wednesday morning.

Congress had overridden an earlier veto of the farm bill last month, despite lawmakers’ discovery that 34 pages were missing from the version originally sent to the White House.

In rejecting the latest version, Bush said he objected to its continued subsidies for wealthy recipients and its use of budgetary gimmicks to conceal a $20 billion increase in spending. But Sen. Kent Conrad, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, said the measure would actually save the government $110 million.

“This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for,” Conrad said. “That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office.”

The discovery of the missing section, Title III, raised concerns among House Republicans that the override vote was improper. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the portions of the bill originally sent to the president became law after Congress voted to override Bush’s first veto. But to put Title III into effect, Congress re-passed the entire bill, including the missing pages, and sent it again to Bush.

The House voted 306-110 at the end of May. The Senate approved the bill 77-15 at the beginning of June.

Two-thirds of the farm bill’s $300 billion in spending will go to nutrition programs such as food stamps. Another $40 billion will be directed toward farm subsidies, while $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle and for other environmental programs.

After vetoing the latest version of the farm bill, Bush on Wednesday criticized Congress for failing to “modify certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message.”

When he vetoed the first version, Bush said the bill “continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase.” The president also said it would undermine efforts to improve American farmers’ access to overseas markets.

Congress has passed one other bill over Bush’s objections: legislation authorizing a $23 billion water project, which the president vetoed in 2007.

CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Wednesday, Congress again enacted a $300 billion farm bill despite President Bush’s veto, repeating the process because a clerical mistake had affected the earlier version of the legislation.

Lawmakers overturned Bush’s second veto of the farm measure after the Senate voted 80-14 to pass it over his objections. That followed a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. In both chambers, the margins comfortably exceeded the two-thirds threshold required to override a presidential veto, which Bush had issued Wednesday morning.

Congress had already overridden a previous Bush veto of the same farm bill the month before, even though lawmakers later found that the copy originally delivered to the White House was missing 34 pages.

In rejecting the revised bill, Bush said he remained opposed to subsidies that benefit wealthy recipients and criticized what he called budget maneuvers used to conceal a $20 billion rise in spending.

Sen. Kent Conrad, the Democratic chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, disputed that criticism, saying the legislation would actually reduce government costs by $110 million.

“This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for,” Conrad said. “That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office.”

The missing portion, known as Title III, raised questions among House Republicans about whether the first override vote had been valid. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi argued that the parts of the bill initially sent to the president became law once Congress overrode Bush’s first veto. However, to ensure Title III also took effect, Congress passed the full legislation again, this time with the omitted pages included, and sent it back to Bush.

The House approved the corrected bill 306-110 in late May, and the Senate followed with a 77-15 vote in early June.

Of the farm bill’s $300 billion in spending, about two-thirds is directed to nutrition assistance programs, including food stamps. An additional $40 billion is designated for farm subsidies, while $30 billion is set aside for payments to farmers who leave land unused and for other environmental initiatives.

After vetoing the newest version, Bush criticized Congress on Wednesday for failing to alter what he described as “objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions,” adding, “I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message.”

When Bush vetoed the first version, he said the measure “continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase.” He also argued that the bill would undermine efforts to expand U.S. farmers’ access to foreign markets.

This marked only the second time Congress passed legislation over Bush’s objections. The other instance involved a $23 billion water projects bill that Bush vetoed in 2007.

CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

Congress gave final approval to a roughly $300 billion farm bill, overriding President George W. Bush’s veto for the second time after a clerical mistake forced lawmakers to repeat part of the process.

The unusual situation began when Congress first sent the farm legislation to the White House, but the enrolled version was missing 34 pages because of a clerical error. President Bush vetoed that version, and Congress voted to override him. Because the text sent to the president was incomplete, however, lawmakers moved to correct the mistake by passing the full bill again in both the House and the Senate, sending the corrected measure back to the White House, and then overriding Bush’s veto once more.

The bill passed with overwhelming bipartisan support, reflecting the broad political backing farm legislation often receives from rural-state lawmakers, anti-hunger advocates, and members concerned with conservation programs. Supporters argued that the measure was necessary to maintain the nation’s farm safety net, expand nutrition assistance, and fund environmental programs. They also said the bill was paid for under congressional budget rules and represented a fiscally responsible compromise.

President Bush opposed the legislation, saying it spent too much money and continued subsidies for farmers at a time when commodity prices were high and farm incomes were strong. The administration had pushed for deeper reforms to farm payments and objected to benefits going to some higher-income producers. Bush also criticized the overall cost of the bill and said it did not do enough to modernize federal farm policy.

Despite those objections, large majorities in both chambers voted to enact the bill over the president’s veto. The legislation directed major funding toward food and nutrition programs, including assistance for low-income families, while also continuing farm commodity subsidies, crop support programs, and conservation initiatives designed to protect environmentally sensitive land and encourage better land-management practices.

counterfactuals.output:
**Congress overrides Bush veto of $300 billion farm bill despite clerical error**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Congress voted Thursday to override President George W. Bush’s veto of a roughly $300 billion farm bill, handing the White House a major legislative defeat even as lawmakers scrambled to address an embarrassing clerical error that left part of the bill out of the version sent to the president.

The House and Senate each voted by wide margins to override Bush’s veto, preserving a sweeping five-year measure that funds farm subsidies, nutrition programs, conservation initiatives and rural development projects.

But the victory was complicated by a mistake in the formal enrollment of the legislation: A section of the bill was accidentally omitted before it was sent to the White House. The missing portion included trade-related provisions, prompting questions about whether the bill Bush vetoed — and Congress overrode — was the same measure lawmakers had passed.

Democratic leaders said they would move quickly to fix the problem by passing the full bill again and, if necessary, overriding another veto.

The farm bill had drawn strong bipartisan support in Congress, particularly from lawmakers representing agricultural states. Supporters said the legislation was essential to farmers and ranchers and also expanded food assistance at a time of rising grocery prices.

Bush opposed the bill, arguing that it spent too much and continued subsidies for wealthy farmers at a time when farm incomes were strong.

In his veto message, Bush said the legislation “continues subsidies for the wealthy” and failed to reform federal farm programs. The administration also criticized the bill’s cost and said it relied on budget gimmicks.

Still, Congress moved quickly to reject the veto. The House voted first, easily exceeding the two-thirds majority required. The Senate followed with its own override vote.

The clerical error created an unusual procedural tangle. Because the enrolled bill sent to Bush was missing pages, lawmakers faced uncertainty over whether the enacted law included the omitted section. Congressional aides said the error was inadvertent and occurred during the preparation of the final document.

Despite the confusion, leaders in both chambers insisted the core of the bill would become law.

The measure includes billions of dollars for crop supports, conservation programs and nutrition assistance, including food stamps. It also contains aid for specialty crops, disaster assistance and energy programs intended to encourage biofuels and other rural energy development.

The override marked one of the rare times Congress successfully overturned a veto by Bush, who had used his veto power sparingly during much of his presidency but increasingly clashed with the Democratic-controlled Congress in his final years in office.

WASHINGTON — Congress on Wednesday overrode President George W. Bush’s second veto of the five-year farm bill, ending an unusual legislative detour caused when lawmakers discovered that a section on trade and international food aid had been left out of the version originally sent to the White House.

The House voted 317-109 to override the veto, comfortably exceeding the two-thirds majority required. The Senate followed with an 80-14 vote, completing enactment of the full farm bill over Bush’s objections.

Bush vetoed the measure earlier in the day, repeating his criticism that the bill was too costly and did too little to reform farm subsidies. The White House said the legislation continued payments to wealthy farmers at a time of high crop prices and included tax and spending provisions the administration opposed.

The farm bill, estimated at roughly $300 billion over five years, renews and revises federal agriculture, nutrition, conservation, energy and rural development programs. The largest share of the spending is for nutrition programs, including food stamps, which account for about two-thirds of the bill — more than $200 billion over five years. Commodity supports for crops such as corn, wheat, rice, cotton and soybeans make up roughly $40 billion, while conservation programs account for about $25 billion. The measure also includes funding for crop insurance, renewable energy, specialty crops, rural development and agricultural research.

The vote was the second time in a month that Congress moved to override Bush on the legislation. In May, the House and Senate voted to override his veto of the farm bill, but officials later discovered that Title III — the trade title — had been inadvertently omitted from the enrolled bill sent to the president.

That missing section included provisions dealing with agricultural trade, export credit programs and international food aid, including food-for-peace and school feeding programs. Because the Constitution requires the president to act on the exact bill passed by Congress, the omission created uncertainty over whether the full measure had been properly enacted.

To correct the error, congressional leaders repassed the complete bill with all 15 titles included and sent it again to Bush. The president vetoed it again, and both chambers again voted to override him.

Supporters of the bill, including farm-state lawmakers from both parties, said it provided needed stability for producers while expanding nutrition assistance and conservation efforts. Opponents said Congress missed an opportunity to impose deeper limits on subsidy payments and modernize farm policy.

# Congress Overrides Bush’s 2008 Farm Bill Veto

Congress delivered a major bipartisan rebuke to President George W. Bush in May 2008, overriding his veto of the $300 billion farm bill and enacting the legislation despite White House objections over spending and subsidy policy.

The House voted **316–108** to override the veto, comfortably exceeding the two-thirds majority required. The Senate followed with an **82–13** vote, completing the override and making the bill law.

Bush had argued that the legislation was too expensive and insufficiently reformed farm policy. He objected to continuing subsidies for some prosperous farmers at a time of high crop prices and rising farm incomes, and he criticized the bill for what he described as budget gimmicks and misplaced priorities. The administration said the bill expanded spending while failing to target aid to farmers who most needed it.

Democratic leaders defended the measure as a broad rural and nutrition package, not simply a subsidy bill. House Speaker **Nancy Pelosi** said the bill addressed national priorities by supporting farmers, expanding food and nutrition assistance, promoting conservation, and investing in renewable energy. She framed the override as a response to the needs of both rural communities and families facing higher food costs.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman **Kent Conrad** also challenged Bush’s fiscal criticism. Citing the **Congressional Budget Office**, Conrad argued that the bill was paid for under congressional budget rules and would not worsen the deficit. He said CBO’s analysis showed the measure was fiscally responsible compared with simply extending existing farm programs.

The override reflected the farm bill’s unusually broad coalition: farm-state lawmakers from both parties, anti-hunger advocates, conservation groups, and renewable energy supporters. Although Bush’s veto highlighted long-running disputes over agricultural subsidies and federal spending, the lopsided votes in both chambers showed that Congress had more than enough support to enact the bill over his opposition.

**Congress Overrides Bush Veto of Sweeping Farm Bill, Delivering Bipartisan Rebuke**

**WASHINGTON —** Congress handed President George W. Bush a significant election-year defeat by overriding his veto of a sweeping farm bill that expands nutrition assistance, preserves a broad system of crop subsidies, and increases funding for environmental conservation programs.

The override marked a rare but decisive bipartisan rejection of the president’s fiscal and policy objections. The House voted overwhelmingly to enact the measure over Bush’s veto, followed by a similarly lopsided Senate vote, easily clearing the two-thirds threshold required in both chambers.

The legislation, a multiyear farm and food policy package costing hundreds of billions of dollars, extends programs that affect farmers, low-income families, rural communities, land conservation, and agricultural markets. While commonly called the “farm bill,” the largest share of its funding goes not to crop payments but to nutrition programs, particularly food stamps.

Bush vetoed the bill after arguing that it was too expensive, too generous to wealthy farmers, and insufficiently reformed. He criticized Congress for continuing subsidies at a time of high crop prices and strong farm incomes, saying the bill failed to impose meaningful limits on payments to large agricultural producers.

Lawmakers from both parties rejected that argument, saying the bill represented a negotiated compromise that balanced farm-state priorities with expanded food aid and conservation measures.

### Nutrition Funding at the Center of the Bill

A major portion of the legislation is devoted to nutrition assistance, including food stamps, emergency food programs, and support for low-income families facing rising grocery costs.

The bill increases nutrition spending by billions of dollars over its lifespan. It raises benefits for many recipients, improves eligibility rules, and strengthens programs aimed at food banks and school-age children. It also renames the food stamp program the **Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program**, or SNAP, reflecting an effort to modernize and reduce stigma around the benefit.

Supporters said the nutrition provisions were especially urgent as food prices climbed and economic strains deepened for working families.

“This bill is not just about farmers,” backers argued during debate. “It is about families trying to put food on the table.”

### Farm Subsidies Preserved Despite Reform Push

The legislation continues traditional farm supports, including direct payments, price-based assistance, crop insurance, and disaster-related programs for producers of major commodities such as corn, wheat, cotton, rice, and soybeans.

Bush had pressed for stricter limits on subsidies, particularly payments to high-income individuals and large farming operations. The final bill does tighten some eligibility standards, but not nearly as much as the administration wanted.

Critics, including fiscal conservatives and some urban lawmakers, said the measure missed an opportunity to overhaul a subsidy system they view as outdated and inequitable. They argued that record commodity prices weakened the case for continuing generous federal support.

Farm-state lawmakers countered that the safety net remains essential because agriculture is vulnerable to volatile markets, bad weather, fuel costs, and global competition. They also emphasized that subsidy provisions were only one piece of a much broader bill.

### Environmental and Conservation Payments Expanded

The farm bill also boosts funding for environmental programs that pay farmers and ranchers to conserve land, improve water quality, protect wetlands, reduce erosion, and adopt more sustainable practices.

Conservation provisions include support for programs that encourage farmers to take environmentally sensitive land out of production, preserve grasslands, improve wildlife habitat, and reduce agricultural runoff. These payments are designed to reward land stewardship while keeping farms economically viable.

Environmental groups were divided. Some praised the additional conservation money, while others said the bill still devoted too much to traditional commodity subsidies and not enough to climate, water, and land protection.

### A Second Major Override of Bush

The farm bill override was notable not only for its size but also because veto overrides were uncommon during Bush’s presidency. It followed Congress’s earlier override of his veto of a major water-projects bill, a measure authorizing billions of dollars for flood control, navigation, coastal restoration, and Army Corps of Engineers projects across the country.

That earlier vote was the first successful override of Bush’s presidency and demonstrated Congress’s willingness—especially on legislation with broad local benefits—to defy the White House. The farm bill override reinforced the same dynamic: when a bill distributes benefits across enough states and districts, presidential opposition can be overcome by regional and bipartisan coalitions.

### Political Implications

The override underscored Bush’s weakened leverage with Congress in the final year of his presidency. Although Republicans had often supported his veto threats on spending and tax issues, many GOP lawmakers broke with him on the farm bill because of its importance to rural districts and agricultural states.

Democrats, who controlled Congress, framed the vote as a victory for families, farmers, and rural communities. Republicans who supported the override defended the bill as necessary for economic stability in farm country.

The result was a broad legislative coalition that included liberal Democrats drawn by nutrition and conservation funding, conservative and moderate farm-state Republicans focused on agricultural supports, and members of both parties seeking local benefits.

Despite the president’s objections, Congress’s vote ensured that the farm bill would become law, locking in a major federal commitment to food assistance, farm income support, and conservation policy for years to come.
